analytic.title: Amorphous Dielectric Optical Coatings Deposited by Plasma Ion Assisted Electron Beam Evaporation for Gravitational Wave Detectors

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Coating thermal noise (CTN) in amorphous coatings is a drawback hindering their application in precision experiments such as gravitational wave detectors (GWDs). Mirrors for GWDs are Bragg's reflectors consisting of a bilayer-based stack of high and low refractive index materials showing high reflectivity and low CTN. In this paper, we report the characterisation of morphological, structural, optical, and mechanical properties of high index materials such as scandia (Sc2O3) and hafnia (HfO2) and a low index material such as magnesium fluoride (MgF2) deposited by plasma ion-assisted electron beam evaporation. We also evaluate their properties under different annealing treatments and discuss their potential for GWDs.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Optical interference coatings for gravitational wave detection have to meet a variety of specific requirements, such as low absorption, high reflectance and low mechanical losses, as well as high resistance against damage by power laser radiation, and long-term optical stability [1]. When utilised in gravitational wave detectors (GWDs), material processing for coatings on large and massive suspended mirrors leads to additional problems arising from the requirements of low stress, low density of defects and high uniformity. To that end, the improvement of more reliable and sophisticated thin-film deposition technologies is needed, allowing next generation of GWDs to augment their sensitivity towards the detection of interacting black holes, neutron stars, and even new unpredicted phenomena [2].

High reflecting (HR) coatings utilised in GWDs such as Advanced LIGO, Advanced Virgo and KAGRA consist of Bragg's reflectors alternating layers of low (SiO2, 1.44 < n < 1.48 at l = 1064 nm) and high (TiO2:Ta2O5, n = 2.11 at l = 1064 nm) refractive-index materials and are typically deposited by ion-beam sputtering (IBS) techniques [3]. Reflectivities as high as R > 99.9995% can be achieved with coating mechanical losses of (2.4.0±0.1)×10 -4 rad (annealed TiO2:Ta2O5, with Ti/Ta =0.27 optimal ratio) to (4.5±0.3)×10 -5 rad (SiO2) in the band of 50 to 900 Hz [3], and optical absorption of less than 0.5 ppm (at l = 1064 nm) [4], [5]. Moreover, in this advanced GWDs, coating uniformity on a large scale (better than 99.9% over Ø15 cm diameter) is required [5]. IBS system at LMA has demonstrated great results on Ti-Ta2O5/SiO2 HR coatings, thanks to the use of a sample holder with a planetary motion coupled with a dedicated mask, exhibiting uniformities above 99.8% on Ø16 cm in monolayers, and above 99.95% in HR coatings on Ø24 cm [5]. However, IBS suffers main drawbacks being the unintentional incorporation of Ar bubbles [6] [7] and the excessive oxygen entrapped in the nanobubbles observed in oxide-based films [8], during the deposition process [6] and after annealing processes [9], hindering the optical and mechanical properties of the coating [10] [11]. IBS deposition rates are highly influenced by growth parameters (source settings, reactive atmosphere pressure, bombardment, etc.) showing values ranged between 0.01 nm/s (e.g., for IBS HfO2) [12] or 0.1 nm/s (e.g., for IBS MgF2) [13]. The deposition rates achieved by alternative techniques such as reactive biased target deposition (RBTD) are around an order of magnitude lower than with a gridded IBS system, exhibiting growth rates around 0.0096 nm/s for Sc2O3 [14]. Alternative deposition techniques such as plasma ion assisted electron beam evaporation (PA-EBE) offers the possibility to deposit high quality films preventing the utilisation of Ar (avoiding unwanted bubbles) increasing the deposition rates up to 0.3 nm/s (this work). In this regard, optimisation of the coating design aiming to dilute the loss contribution of the high-index material has been explored through the deposition of new materials and utilisation of deposition techniques different to IBS. The latter includes techniques such as PA-EBE [15], [16], highly promising for producing highly uniform coatings at higher deposition rates than IBS (factor 10) and greatly scalable (needed for the fabrication of mirrors at main GWDs).

Scandium sesquioxide (Sc2O3) or also known as scandia is a high refractive index material who has been presented as a promising material for its use in optical interference coatings in GWDs and other high-power lasers applications (e.g., high power remove laser transmission and optoelectronic functional devices) [17] [18], mainly due to its high bandgap (5.7 eV) [19], which is larger than other high index metal-oxides like HfO2 [20]. Since the theory predicts that the scaling of the laser breakdown fluence with the bandgap, and the utilisation of a dielectric material with a wider band gap energy will prevent laser damage in aforementioned applications [20]. Along with low index materials such as SiO2, though not widely studied, Sc2O3 has been demonstrated in dielectric interference-based mirror coatings developed for high-power ultraviolet (UV) lasers [21]. High optical coatings based on Sc2O3 have been successfully deposited by techniques, including IBS [22], [23], reactive magnetron sputtering (RMS) [24], pulsed laser deposition (PLD) [25], and reactive biased target sputtering deposition (RBTD) [14].

Hafnium dioxide (HfO2) also called hafnia, is a dielectric material characterized by a high refractive index, exhibiting a large laser damage threshold [26] due to a wide bandgap energy of around 5.5 eV [27]. As a result of these properties and its transparency over a wide range in the electromagnetic spectrum, covering from the UV to the mid-IR, is widely utilised in optical coating applications [28] and investigated as promising material GWDs [12]. In contrast to Sc2O3, the optical properties of HfO2 have been extensively studied, however, these studies have offered a variety of conclusions regarding the refractive index and the extinction coefficient [29], [30]. This large scattering of optical constants is originated mainly from the use of different techniques. Among all, both ion-assisted electron beam evaporation and sputtering presented the more compact films with refractive index close to those reported for bulk HfO2 [31], while electron-beam evaporated films demonstrated to have lower refractive index values [32]. This material has been also deposited by atomic layer deposition (ALD) [33][34] RMS [35], and IBS, the latter being characterised at cryogenic conditions, for future GWDs such as Einstein Telescope [36]. In those characterisations, HfO2 presented extremely low loss angles (2-3×10 -4 ) but with Young's modulus values four times higher than that obtained in low-index materials such as SiO2. This dissimilarity found in the Young's modulus values between substrate (SiO2) and coating based on HfO2 lead to increased thermal noise.

Fluoride thin films such as magnesium fluoride (MgF2) are widely used for a wide number of optical applications due to their beneficial characteristics, including a relatively high damage threshold (useful for high power lasers applications), high hardness, good stability in hostile environments, and a very low refractive index (n = 1.38) [37]. However, MgF2 films deposited by means of IBS [13], RMS [38], ion beam assisted deposition (IBAD) and vacuum evaporation techniques at room temperature, the latter resulting in porous columnar microstructure [39].

That is a drawback for mirror coatings since the porous tend to be filled by moisture in room air leading to a detrimental effect on the stability of the coatings through the variation of the optical and mechanical properties of the coating.

This work presents a study of optical and mechanical properties of three potential material candidates to improve the performance of next generation of GWDs, including scandium oxide (Sc2O3, scandia), magnesium fluoride (MgF2, sellaite) and hafnium oxide (HfO2, hafnia). These films were deposited by PA-EBE which is a technique that presents some advantages with respect to standard IBS, including less or zero Ar-gas impurities and material consumption [40]. Moreover, PA-EBE also presents high deposition rates (0.3 nm/s, factor 10 higher than IBS), great thickness control and radial uniformity (in this work: 99.98% uniformity over Ø10.16 cm coatings) being essential for the coating of large test mass in GWDs. PA-EBE also has a good control on the doping through the utilisation of multiple crucibles to control the material mixing during the so-called co-deposition. Good examples of that accurate doping control are metal oxide films, e.g., 0.5-2wt% in doped titanium oxide [41] and 0.6-5wt% in doped indium oxides [42].

div.head: Deposition of thin films
div.p: Single layer coatings consisting of 396-nm thick Sc2O3, 345-nm thick MgF2 and 238-nm thick HfO2 were deposited using plasma ion assisted electron beam evaporation (Satis 1200), being a vacuum deposition system with a multi-pocket Temescal electron beam gun (Fig. 1). This work utilizes a novel plasma source based on inductive heating inner and outer surfaces of a lanthanum hexaboride high-efficiency thermionic emitter hollow cathode [43]. In the case of MgF2 films, 1-3 mm pellets (99.99% purity) were utilised. For the deposition of metal oxides, 5-mm drops of Hf with a purity of 99.5%, and 2-mm granules of Sc2O3 with a purity of 99.99% were loaded in a crucible at the PA-EBE system, for their later evaporation using an electron beam (Part 8 in Fig. 1), and oxidized with an oxygen plasma source (Part 7 in Fig. 1). The deposition conditions were optimised using design of experiments (DoE) to determine not only the influence of the growth parameters on the growth rate, but also to find a low deposition rate (thickness control) producing good optical properties (i.e., high n and low k).

The studied deposition parameters comprised the accelerating current (IAC), accelerating volage (VAC), external current (IEX), O2 flux, Ar flux at the cathode (ArCathode), Ar flux at the anode (ArAnode), and the induction power heater. Table 1 summarises the optimised deposition conditions for each coating, as well as resulting e-beam evaporation rates.

div.head: Characterisation of thin films
div.p: Morphological properties of the coatings, including thickness, pinholes density and surface roughness, were analysed by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) at 20 kV (S4100 cold FEG from Hitachi). The amorphous structure of the films was also analysed by grazing-incidence X-ray diffraction (GIXRD) analysis (Siemens D5000, Cu Kα radiation at 40 kV/30 mA). Films composition (i.e., stoichiometry) was analysed by energy dispersive X-ray (EDX) analysis (S4100 cold FEG from Hitachi).

The Satis1200 vacuum chamber was used for coating depositions and plasma characterization.

The schematical chamber layout is shown on Fig. 3.1. Stress measurements were carried out in a Wafer Geometry Gauge system (MX 203-6-33 from E+H Metrology GmbH). 4-inch Si(100) wafers (also called here discs) with a thickness of 0.1 mm were used as substrates. The gauge is a manually loaded wafer geometry measuring instrument for round wafers (mainly silicon wafers, but open to other materials as well). This equipment is dedicated to control the thickness and shape of wafers, as well as evaluation of the average stress calculated from the local stress measured across the wafer, key for this work.

E+H Metrology system, like other wafer geometry instruments, uses a contactless capacitive distance sensor to determine aforementioned parameters (see more details in Section A of Supplementary information). The MX-NT and Wafer Studio software were used to carry out the measurements and for the visualization and data analysis, respectively. Fig. 2 shows the calculation of stress from pre-measurements and post measurements carried out in a blank disc and a coated disc, respectively. Coating stress varies across the area of the coating which is known as the local stress which is influenced by material type and deposition method. Factors such as orientation of the wafer in the coating chamber, substrate rotation, reactive gas angle of delivery and other process parameters can all effect the local stress values and will result in a deviation from radial symmetry. In addition, the irregular starting geometry of a wafer will also mean that a perfect radial symmetry in local coating stress is unlikely to be observed.

The local the local stress represented in Fig. 2(b) has symmetry across the y-axis and a separate symmetry across the x-axis. This symmetry mirrors the local thickness deviation of the wafer which is represented in Fig. 2(a) so it is a reasonable assumption to make, that the main contributing factor to local stress variation is from the local thickness variation inherent to the coated wafer. div.head: Morphological characterisation
div.p: A visual inspection of the coatings deposited by plasma ion assisted electron beam evaporation on a 4-inch Si(100) wafer showed a uniform film over the large area of the substrate (Fig. 4(a)).

SEM analysis of the films demonstrated an amorphous morphology in the three materials under study (Fig. 4(b-d)). These results are in good agreement with those obtained by XRD analysis (see diffractograms in the next section). Moreover, the analysis of the coatings by optical microscopy also confirmed the absence of pinholes in the resulting films, making these coatings to be presented as a great candidate for high reflecting mirrors. SEM images of the film cross section (Fig. 4(e-g)) probed the high uniformity achieved over large areas (wafer scale) during the PA-EBE deposition of the films. Coating uniformity was evaluated by mapping the large area of the 4-inch coated wafer, analysing the cross-section of 12 different points of the wafer (see Section C in Supplementary Material). Results conclude a variation of that thickness below 0.03% (HfO2), 0.02% (MgF2) and 0.02% (Sc2O3), meaning a thickness uniformity above 99.97%, 99.98%, and 99.98%, for the HfO2, MgF2 and Sc2O3 coatings, respectively. Considering the requirement for future GWDs of thickness uniformities better than 99.9% over Ø15 cm diameter [5], these results make PA-EBE to be a promising technique for producing HR uniform coatings at wafer scale.

div.head: Structural analysis
div.p: XRD analysis was used to characterise the structure of the films right after their deposition (Before Annealing, BA) and after annealing treatments carried out for 2 hours at different temperatures ranged between 100 and 700 o C. Fig. 5 (a-c) demonstrates highly amorphous films before the annealing treatment, in good agreement with SEM observations of the surface morphology (Fig. 4). To attribute the crystalline phase(s), the positions of Bragg peaks were compared to the International Centre for Diffraction Database (ICDD).

BA, Sc2O3 exhibited a broad peak centred around 31.561 o , identified with a star (☆) in Fig. 5(a) which could correspond to the (222) diffraction plane in the Sc2O3 structure (ICDD card no. 00-005-0629) [50]. The large full width at half maximum (FWHM) of this peak evidenced the amorphous characteristic of the PA-EBE Sc2O3 film. This FWHM was observed not to be affected by the annealing temperature, in contrast to its intensity, whose value was increased by this treatment. This result indicated that some level of crystal order was produced by the thermal treatment and was greatly visible at temperatures above 400 o C. Fig. 5 (a) also showed other peaks labelled with circle (○) corresponding to the diffraction peaks from the Si substrate.
This was confirmed by the characterisation of pristine Si(100) substrate in the same conditions (i.e., after the same thermal treatments).

div.head: Compositional study
div.p: Table 2 summarises the compositional analysis of the three coatings. The table provides the atomic ratio of each binary compound defined as AxBy, where A and B correspond to the cations and anions, respectively, and y/x is the anion to cation ratio. The stoichiometric column presents the ideal y/x for each of the compounds. For comparison, the table also shows the y/x obtained by other deposition techniques utilised to synthesize the sample three materials. From the comparison, it is observed that PA-EBE produced non-stoichiometric coatings, exhibiting oxygen excess in both hafnia and scandia (over stoichiometric), and fluor deficit in the magnesium fluoride coating (under stoichiometric). Compared to other techniques such as atomic layer deposition (ALD) [33], reactive magnetron sputtering (RMS) [35], IBS [36], and RBTD [12], exhibiting HfO2 stoichiometric films (i.e., y/x of around 2.00), PA-EBE used in this work resulted in over stoichiometric films. Further depositions using design of experiments (DoE) will allow to determine the role of oxygen on the resulting film stoichiometry, and thus, to tune the stoichiometry of the coatings. Similarly, Sc2O3 films deposited in this work, presented a y/x value around 2.1, being above the stochiometric films achieved by ALD [33] [34], RMS [24], PLD [25], and RBTD [14]. In the case of MgF2, the under stoichiometric values obtained here of 1.7 are slightly lower to those reported with EBE (1.95), but close to those obtained by RMS and IBS [13].

In spite of this drastic difference in the composition of the films did not affect the amorphous characteristics of the resulting coatings as demonstrated by SEM and XRD, however, it had a high impact on the mechanical and optical properties of the three materials as it will be presented later on. 2.00 (ALD) [33] 1.96 (RMS) [35] 2.00 (RBTD) [12] 2.00 (IBS) [36] MgxFy 2.0 1.7

div.head: Stress measurements
div.p: The stress value obtained in Sc2O3 films around 32.19 MPa, indicates a tensile stress which is orders of magnitudes lower than those reported for IBS Sc2O3 films (range of GPa) the latter caused by the high density of oxygen interstitials produced by that Ar based IBS method [53].

MgF2 films evaporated in this work exhibit 150 MPa. This result evidence a tensile stress lower than those reported in the literature (550 MPa) [54]. The origin of that stress reduction could be due to the benefits of plasma ion assisted method used here, contributing to decline the density of isolated crystalline aggregates, leading to the increase of the partial disorder in the resulting structure. Tensile stress values of 118 MPa obtained for HfO2 are in good agreement with the 115 MPa obtained for 260-nm thick HfO2 e-beam evaporated films reported in the literature, indicating that the layer could have reached a low level of porosity of around 9.4% [55]. In this regard, the porosity of coatings deposited by direct evaporation, EBE and IBS techniques has been thoroughly studied [56]. In those studies, it has been demonstrated that the utilisation of plasma or ion assistance during the depositions produced an improvement of the coating densities towards the bulk material, resulting in larger refractive index, better mechanical and structural properties. The studies also showed that IBS produces more compact films, with higher refractive index compared to EBE and hence less porosity. The low stress obtained in PA-EBE coatings deposited here, indicates the benefit of the plasma assistance to reduce the porosity and improve both mechanical and optical properties.

div.head: Coating mechanical loss
div.p: Table 3 shows the resulting mechanical loss angles measured by GeNS system (Fig. 3(a)), including substrate (fsubstrate) and coated (fcoated) loss obtained from ringdown measurements (Fig. 3(b)) and Eq(1). The table also includes the coating (fcoating) loss calculated by using the substrate/coating energy ratio (Es/Ec) obtained in ANSYS and Eq (2). An extended version of this table including results obtained in a second GeNS system available at University of Strathclyde (UoS) could be found in the supplementary information (see Section D) showing a fair agreement with the results showed in Table 3. For the sake of clarity, the fsubstrate, fcoated and fcoating loss angles summarised in Table 3 are also presented in Fig. 6 (a). In that figure, it is observed the low loss exhibited by the silica substrates (blue triangles) after their annealing at 1000 o C (releasing any accumulated stress).
The figure also shows fcoated for the three materials in the range of 10 -6 . Subtracting the effect of the substrate, and considering the Es/Ec energy ratio (Eq(2)), one could obtain the fcoating.

The low fcoating values of 4.1×10 -4 obtained in Sc2O3 films make the evaporation method used here to be promising a technique for high index Sc2O3 based coatings (Fig. 6 (a)). All the coatings show an approximate constant dependence of the fcoating with respect to the resonant frequency. Among all, MgF2 is the coating exhibiting fcoating in the range of 10 -3 (Fig.

MgF2 coatings deposited by different techniques showed fcoating of (5.5-7.5)×10 -4 at 2.5-39 kHz (IBS technique) [13] and (3.5-5.0)×10 -4 at 30 Hz (thermal evaporation) [57] which highlights the different nature of the resulting thin films grown with a different technique.

Fig. 6 (c) presents high fcoating for HfO2 ranged between (7-19)×10 -3 . In contrast, IBS HfO2 coatings presented lower loss values ranged between (0.9-1)×10 -3 and even lower when coatings were subjected to annealing treatments as it will be discussed later on [36]. Those fcoating could be further reduced by the application of thermal annealing below the crystallisation temperature [1] [36], and the optimisation of the evaporation conditions (mainly through the increase of the ion energy and reduced deposition rate). As such, coating loss was measured for each material after various thermal treatments carried out for 2 hours at 100, 200, 300, and 400 o C. The results of the experiment are summarised in Fig. 6 (d-f) with outcomes from the annealing study resulted in a beneficial impact on all coating losses. It is observed in Fig. 6 (d-f) how the loss angle decreases as the temperature of the annealing increases. This provides indirect evidence of the reduction of defects density within the structure of the coatings, preventing the dissipation of the energy during the Q-factor measurements. Analysing case by case, it is found that for the Sc2O3 coating, the fundamental mode, showing the minimum fcoating of 4.1×10 -4 further reduced its value down to 3.05×10 -4 after an annealing treatment of 400 o C for 2 hours. Annealing treatments in MgF2 coatings did produce a reduction of the fcoating in all the modes under analysis, however, their values were still in the 10 -3 range (Fig. 6 (e)). Finally, HfO2 exhibited a drastic reduction of fcoating due to the thermal effects brining the fcoating down to 4×10 -4 (Fig. 6 (f)) which is close to the 3×10 -4 reported for RBTD HfO2 annealed at 650 o C for 10 hours (0.3×10 -4 ) [12], but till one order of magnitude higher than those reported for IBS HfO2 coatings annealed at 400 o C for 24 hours [36]. However, although the HfO2 presents a very low mechanical loss (lower than most of the h-index metal oxides proposed by GWDs) its high Young's modulus values are four times higher than that of SiO2. This dissimilar Young's modulus values between substrate (SiO2) and coating is expected to lead to increased thermal noise [12].

div.head: Optical properties (a) (b) (c) (d) (e) (f)
div.p: T and R spectra (Fig. 7 (a)) have been used to calculate refractive index (n) of coatings as a function of the wavelength using the Sellmeier expression (Fig. 7 (b)). Results obtained at l = 1064 nm show n of 1.75 (Sc2O3), 1.33 (MgF2) and 1.89 (HfO2). The extinction coefficient in the evaporated films is below the detection limit of the spectrophotometer instrument over the wavelength range of inspection (measurable extinction coefficients higher than 10 -3 ). Further optimisation of n needs to be performed through increased plasma source outpution energy during the evaporation process [4,12]. Table 4 compares the optical constants obtained here (Fig. 7 (b)) with those reported in the literature. HfO2 showed a high index of 1.89 in a good agreement with those results obtained with the same technique [59] and slightly lower than those reported by PIAD (1.95) [45] and IBS (2.09) [12][44]. In the case of PIAD, the optimisation of the applied voltage during the deposition process benefited to the resulting optical constant, similarly to the effects on the absorption (as it will be described later on). Among the three, IBS showed the highest refractive index which evidences a more compact and less porous structure, close to the bulk HfO2 material.

Sc2O3 films presented a moderated high index still far from those reported by sputtering systems such as IBS (1.95) [46] and RMS (1.91-1.97) [60], the latter highly subjected to changes in the stoichiometry of the ScxOy film. Based on that report, and using the evidence extracted from EDX analysis (see Table 2), the EBE process needs to be optimised in order to improve the stoichiometry of the films, improving the optical properties.

The results presented in Fig. 8(a-c) correspond to the fit to visible wavelength reflectance spectra for single layer coatings on silicon wafer substrate. Refractive index data was obtained using the envelope method and then fit to a 2-oscillator Sellmeier model. The experimental method and the model used here could show slight differences with respect to the dispersive curves presented in Table 4 due to the use of different substrate (glass), and R and T measurements. In this regard, the results discussed in this section will be compared between each other to find the influence of the temperature on the optical constants.

A closer inspection of wavelengths around 1064 nm shows interesting effects of the annealing on the optical properties of the coatings. For example, in the particular case of Sc2O3 (Fig. 8(d)), the refractive index increases with the temperature reaching values around 1.958 which are higher than those reported for IBS and close to record values reported for RMS (see Table 4). MgF2 coatings showed a reduction from 1.35 down to 1.31 (Fig. 8(e)), being greatly beneficial to reduce the number of bi-layers in mirror coatings of GWDs. These values are extremely low compared to those obtained by other technique such as IBAD and evaporation, and close to the record values showed by KMS (see Table 4). Finally, the results obtained for HfO2 evidence a high dependence of n with respect to the annealing temperature (Fig. 8(f)).

The best results were observed at temperatures of 100 o C, where the n reached the maximum values of 1.908. Higher temperatures were demonstrated to produce a negative impact on the refractive index. The variations of the refractive index observed in Fig. 8 were compared against the thickness obtained also from the fitting. Fig. 9 shows the thickness of each coating, including Sc2O3 (Fig. 9 8(a,d). In the case of MgF2 coating, due to the opposite behaviour observed in the n vs temperature curves measured at lower and higher wavelengths Fig. 8(b), it is hard to extract conclusions from Fig. 9(b). In contrast, HfO2 presents a similar trend than that exhibited by Sc2O3, with a reduction of the thickness as the annealing temperature increases (Fig. 9(c)). That reduction was estimated to be lower than in the case of Sc2O3 (only 2.5%), but it is in good agreement also with the results presented in Fig. 8(f), where lower temperatures resulted in higher refractive index (i.e., more compact film) than those observed at higher temperatures (less dense films). Absorption measurements have been carried out on Sc2O3, HfO2 and MgF2 samples at 1064nm using PCI (Fig. 10). The colour line shows the absorption signal expressed in ppm for scanning the position of the coating through the beam crossing point at which the absorption signal reaches a maximum. These absorption measurements are known as 'z-scans', i.e., translating the coating thickness/sample through the interaction region between respective waists of the pump and probe lasers [63], [64]. The magnitude of the maximum in the absorption scan i.e., the central peak is then directly the optical absorption in ppm presented in The mean value for the absorption of measurements taken at different positions on the disc is summarised in Table 5. That table also presents a comparison with absorption values measured in similar coatings but deposited using other techniques. From the comparison, one could conclude that our coatings showed slightly higher absorption than other deposited by PIAD or IBS. In the particular case of HfO2, standard deposition of coatings using PIAD at lower applied voltages below 140 V, showed absorptions close to 30 ppm. The increase of the applied voltage above 140 showed a decrease of the absorption down to 13 ppm (with an increase of the refractive index around 2) [45]. That strategy is a promising route also applicable in our deposition technique to further improve the optical properties of the coatings.

Sc2O3 coatings deposited in this work exhibited values of absorption of around 16 ppm, which are lower than those obtained by IBS techniques [46]. For the case of MgF2, the PA-EBE used here needs further optimisation since the absorption of around 840 ppm is three orders of magnitudes above the requirements of current and future GWDs, making this lowindex material to be not viable as optical coating. and HfO2 films were deposited by ion plasma assisted electron beam evaporation, showing tensile stress of 32, 115 and 150 MPa, significantly lower than coatings deposited by IBS. SEM confirmed the lack of crystalline aggregates and other defects which are the main responsible in IBS coatings increasing the film stress. EDX evidenced that PA-EBE produced non-stoichiometric coatings, exhibiting oxygen excess in both hafnia and scandia (over stoichiometric), and fluor deficit in the magnesium fluoride coating (under stoichiometric). The analysis of the crystalline structure by GIXRD confirmed the amorphous properties of all the coatings. Thermal treatment of the Sc2O3 and MgF2 coatings up to 700 o C did not show relevant crystallization in all the coatings; in contrast, HfO2 coatings exhibited both (120) and (200) diffraction peaks at temperatures >500 o C. Optical characterisation of the films demonstrates high n of 1.75 and 1.89 for Sc2O3 and HfO2 and low n of 1.33 for MgF2 comparable to those reported in the literature for similar coatings deposited by IBS. Annealing of the coatings, showed an increase of n in the high index materials and a reduction of this constant for the low index one. The characterisation of fcoating in those films resulted in values in the range of 10 -4 (Sc2O3) and 10 -3 (MgF2 and HfO2) without the application of any thermal treatment. Upon thermal treatments, coating loss showed a reduction with the temperature, exhibiting best values for all the coatings at 400 o C. Moreover, annealing treatments produced an improvement of coatings optical properties through the increase of n in Sc2O3 and HfO2 coatings up to of 1.959 (400 o C) and 1.908 (100 o C), respectively, and the decrease of the n in MgF2 films down to 1.315 (300 o C). A further optimisation of the optical and mechanical properties is possible through ion energy enhancement by increasing the acceleration voltage in the plasma ion assisted electron beam evaporation and/or reducing deposition rate. Future steps will also involve PCI measurements in annealed samples and spectrophotometry at 1550 and 2000 nm for the investigation of these coatings as potential h-and low-index material for HR coatings in future GWDs.
